Beneath the central library, where the pipes ticked like patient insects, Nora found a door that had never been there before. She had worked in the building for eleven years and could identify its moods by sound: the radiators knocking before snow, the high windows sighing in August, the front doors shuddering whenever someone entered against the wind. Yet this narrow door, set behind the map cabinets, was unfamiliar. Its paint was the blue of deep water. A brass plate read UNSAID. Nora touched the letters. Somewhere inside, hundreds of wings began, softly and at once, to tremble in answer.

She opened it. The room beyond was circular and impossibly tall, its walls lined with empty glass jars. Above her, moths covered the ceiling like a second, breathing plaster. Each one was pale as paper, and each, when it stirred, whispered in a human voice. An old man sat beneath them, mending a net with silver thread. “You took your time,” he said. Nora asked what the place was. He pointed his needle toward her. “A cupboard,” he said. “A harbor. A bad habit. Every sentence swallowed instead of spoken leaves something behind. Most things prefer not to vanish completely.”

Nora laughed because the alternative was to run. The sound startled several moths loose. They circled her head, offering fragments: not tonight; after the baby; if you loved me; please don’t; I meant to. One landed on the old man’s sleeve and said, quite clearly, your turn. He folded it into his hand with unexpected tenderness. “People imagine silence is empty,” he told her. “Only because they have never had to carry it.” He rose and took a jar from the lowest shelf. Unlike the others, it was not empty. Inside, a single moth beat slowly against the curved glass.

The instant Nora saw it, she knew. Five years earlier, on the platform after their father’s funeral, her sister had asked whether she would be all right. Clara’s suitcase stood between them. Beyond the windows, a train drew in through rain. Nora had been thirty-four, fiercely competent, exhausted, and furious at being left with the house, the bills, the sympathy casseroles. She had answered, of course. What she had meant to say was no. What she had wanted to say, with a need so large it frightened her, was stay. The moth opened its wings. Nora heard her own voice.

“It has waited longer than most,” the keeper said. “You may take it, but a sentence cannot live forever in a jar. Give it to the person it belongs to before morning, or let it go.” Nora thought of Clara’s last postcard, received eighteen months ago: a yellow doorway, four lines about the weather, no return address except the city she already knew. She thought of their careful messages on birthdays, each one polished until nothing sharp remained. “And if speaking changes nothing?” she asked. The keeper threaded his needle again. “Then you will have changed the silence around you.”

Upstairs, the library had settled into night. Rain darkened the tall windows, and the reading lamps made small gold islands on empty tables. Nora sat at the front desk with the jar beside the telephone. Twice she dialed Clara’s number and hung up before it rang. The third time, she listened to the distant pulse and watched the moth grow still. When her sister answered, suspicion gave way quickly to concern. “Nora? What’s happened?” Nothing, Nora almost said. Instead, she unscrewed the lid. “Do you remember the station?” A pause. “I remember you telling me to go, and I went.”

The words struck with their force, but beneath them Nora heard something she had missed before: bewilderment. She pressed her fingers against the desk. “I wasn’t all right,” she said. “I wanted you to stay. I thought if I asked, you would refuse, and then I would know you had chosen everything else. So I refused for you.” The moth rose from the jar. It did not fly away but rested on the receiver, trembling with each breath. Clara was quiet so long that Nora imagined oceans filling the line. Her sister said, “I waited outside your house that night.”

Nora saw it suddenly: the unlit porch, Clara standing beyond the gate, both of them waiting for the other to become possible. “Why didn’t you knock?” she whispered. “Why didn’t you look outside?” There was anger in it, and grief, but also a startled laugh from Clara, wet and familiar. For a while they passed the blame between them like a heavy chair, each trying to set it down without crushing her own foot. Then they stopped. The moth lifted, circled the lamp, and vanished into its brightness. Nora did not feel forgiven. She felt, more usefully, present at last.

They talked until the rain thinned. Not about everything: the house remained sold, their father remained dead, and certain sentences had acquired scar tissue that would not soften in one night. But Clara described her narrow kitchen and the lemon tree surviving on her balcony. Nora admitted she hated casseroles. They laughed at that with disproportionate helplessness. Before hanging up, Clara said she would come in spring, if spring was not too far away. “It isn’t,” Nora said, though winter had only begun. Afterward, she carried the empty jar downstairs, half expecting the blue door to be gone by then.

It was there. The old keeper slept in his chair, the net across his knees, while far overhead the moths murmured their unfinished weather. Nora set the empty jar on the shelf and understood that she would never learn which silences were mercies and which were small rooms without air. Perhaps no one could. Outside, buses exhaled at the curb and a baker raised his shutters. She walked slowly home through the washed streets, tired in a cleaner way. She had imagined courage as a door swinging open. It was smaller: a voice, unsteady but audible, asking someone to stay.
